title: 5 Shifts I Made in my Phonemic Awareness Instruction
author: Holly Price
summary: A primary teacher describes how a screener showing 79% of her students below grade level in phoneme segmentation pushed her to change a program she was already following. Her shifts were using colored tiles to represent sounds and fading them once most students could segment unaided, concentrating on segmenting and blending rather than rhyming or syllable counting, and adding her own words that matched the current phonics sequence. She also previewed upcoming phonics patterns orally and kept returning to data to spiral in tricky concepts. The piece is a practitioner account rather than research, but the moves are concrete, data-driven and tied to explicit phonics instruction. She reports all students reaching grade level on the measure by year's end.
points: Screening data, not the published program, drove the changes: 79% of students were below grade level in phoneme segmentation at the start.
Colored tiles make sounds physical and the teacher can see student thinking from across the room; they are faded once students can segment without them.
Daily segmenting and blending of 5-10 words beats broader phonological activities like rhyming for moving results.
Adding words aligned to the current phonics scope and sequence, and previewing upcoming patterns orally, connects phonemic awareness to what students are learning to read and spell.
quotes: After administering the screener and looking at the results, I was taken aback with the PSF (Phoneme Segmentation Fluency) scores. Seventy-nine percent of my students were far below or below grade level.

If using manipulatives helped me understand how to break apart the sounds, I knew I needed to try this with my students immediately. I gave each of my students 5 colored tiles to keep in their desks so we could use them when needed.

After giving the middle of the year screener and seeing how 75% of students were able to segment the sounds without manipulatives, I started fading them away and mostly used them for certain students and/or in small groups. Students who were not using manipulatives would show me how many sounds on their fingers.

There is a time and place for practicing things like rhyming words, and counting syllables, but focusing on segmenting and blending every single day helped my class tremendously. Every day we would segment and blend at least 5-10 words.

When I was following Heggarty “with fidelity” it usually did not match what we were doing during the rest of our word study block. I decided to jazz things up by intentionally adding in 3-5 words to segment and blend that aligned with our current phonics instruction.

One easy way I did that during phonemic awareness was adding 2-3 words at least a few times a week with concepts we were going to be studying in the upcoming weeks. It was almost like building some background knowledge before introducing a new phonics concept.
